title: Frisco Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Frisco wells have a median depth of 85 feet, but fractured bedrock can make drilling costs and results vary by lot.
h1: Private Well Guide for Frisco, Colorado
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Frisco means looking closely at the local well record, not just the listing description. Permits within five miles show a median well depth of 85 feet, with the middle half between 46 and 165 feet. The ground is mainly fractured mountain bedrock, so nearby wells can still differ substantially.

Most permitted wells are for domestic or household use, and the reported median yield is 10.0 gallons per minute. That is a useful local benchmark, but only a portion of recorded wells include yield or static-water-level information. Treat the records as a planning guide, then verify the specific parcel, permit history, water rights and site conditions before closing or starting construction.

sections.heading: Frisco well depths reflect shallow records and hard rock
sections.html:
Frisco-area wells are often shallower than buyers expect. The median reported depth is 85 feet, and 55% of wells are under 100 feet. Another 38% fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 7% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 1,000 feet.

That spread matters when you request a drilling bid. A nearby shallow well does not guarantee the same result on your lot because most permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Granite and gneiss can carry water through fractures that change from one location to the next. Use the local middle-half range as a starting point, not a promised drilling depth. Records from Dillon, Silverthorne, Breckenridge and nearby mountain communities can add context, but your immediate neighbors are more useful.

sections.heading: Most Frisco wells report usable household yields
sections.html:
Among wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 7.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The local record shows 63% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 26% reporting more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 11% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

No recorded wells are listed under 1 gallon per minute, but that does not remove the need for a parcel-specific test. Only 510 wells report a pump yield, compared with 2,062 permitted wells in the full record. Ask for the well completion report, pumping test, storage capacity and any production limitations. A household well also needs the correct DWR permit and use terms; the exempt-well pumping limit is 35 gallons per minute.

sections.heading: Water levels in Frisco vary, with no simple decline pattern
sections.html:
The median static water level is 30 feet below the surface, and the middle half is between 15 and 60 feet. That is the depth to water when the well is not being pumped, not the total well depth. It helps with pump planning, trenching and understanding how much water is standing in the casing.

The decade series does not show a steady drop. Median measurements were 15 feet in the 1970s, 50 feet in the 1980s, 70 feet in the 1990s, 52 feet in the 2000s, 35 feet in the 2010s and 18 feet in the 2020s. Because only 176 wells report static water levels, use this as historical context rather than proof of current conditions. Check the date and location of any neighbor measurement.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long activity around Frisco
sections.html:
Well construction around Frisco has a long permit history. The records include 8 permits from the 1950s, 132 from the 1960s, 243 from the 1970s, 233 from the 1980s, 422 from the 1990s, 342 from the 2000s, 187 from the 2010s and 179 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

Of the 2,062 permits, 1,241 are recorded as constructed, while 1,430 report a total depth. The most common use is domestic or household at 69%; monitoring wells make up 19%. In the records, Buena Vista Drilling has 317 wells, Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation has 265, and Authorized (Pe, Pg) has 178. Confirm current licensing, availability and scope directly before hiring.

sections.heading: Frisco drilling costs depend on footage and completion work
sections.html:
Frisco drilling is priced for fractured mountain bedrock, commonly granite or gneiss. The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot for drilling. At the median depth of 85 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $5,500 to $8,500. That is not the finished water system.

With a pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical work, the estimated completed-well range is about $11,500 to $20,500 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, or extra site work can move the bid higher. Ask each driller what is included, how unsuccessful drilling is handled, and whether the price covers testing, permits, pump installation and connection to the house. Compare written scopes rather than only the per-foot number.

sections.heading: Check contamination, dry-hole risk and the building plan
sections.html:
Water quality deserves special attention in a mountain mining area. Within about ten miles of Frisco, the mapped record includes 16 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 515 historic mine features and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These maps do not prove a problem on a particular parcel, but they are a reason to review nearby land uses, mine history and available water-quality results before purchase.

Low yield, a dry hole and difficult access remain practical risks in fractured bedrock. Confirm the septic system location, replacement area, setbacks and building envelope before drilling. A well that works for an existing small home may not support a larger build without reviewing storage, flow and permit conditions. Also check whether an augmentation plan or other water-rights requirement applies to the proposed use in this basin.

sections.heading: What to verify before buying or building near Frisco
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then pull the DWR permit and completion records for neighboring wells. Look for total depth, casing and grout, static water level, yield, pump information and the approved use. The local statistics are helpful, but they are not a guarantee: only 510 wells report yield and 176 report static water level.

For a new build, get a driller to review access, proposed well location, septic layout and the likely drilling interval before you finalize plans. Budget from the complete system range, not only the hole. Ask for a water-quality test suited to the property’s mine and cleanup history. If the parcel is near Dillon, Silverthorne, Breckenridge, Keystone, Copper Mountain or Blue River, use those records for broader context while giving the greatest weight to wells with similar geology and elevation.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Frisco, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Frisco is 85 feet. The middle half runs from 46 to 165 feet. About 55% are under 100 feet, while 38% are between 100 and 300 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss can change sharply between lots, and the deepest recorded well is 1,000 feet.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Frisco?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the 85-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $5,500 to $8,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical work is estimated at $11,500 to $20,500. Access and extra depth can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Frisco wells produce?
faq.a: Reported well yields have a median of 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 7.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 63% between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 26% above 15. Only 510 wells report yield, so request the specific well’s completion and pumping records.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Frisco, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Within about ten miles, the mapped record includes 16 PFAS sites, 515 historic mine features and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These do not prove contamination on your lot. Test the well and review nearby mine, cleanup and land-use history before relying on the water.

faq.q: Do Frisco wells have enough water for a new home?
faq.a: Many reported wells produce household-scale flow, with a 10.0-gallon-per-minute median. Still, only 510 wells include yield data, and fractured bedrock is unpredictable. Confirm the DWR permit, approved use, pumping test, storage and septic layout. New construction may also require review of water rights or an augmentation plan, depending on the proposed use.
